flags.quote: The only orbital parameter with a period near one hundred thousand years is eccentricity, the shape of Earth's orbit, which slides between almost circular and mildly elliptical.
flags.detail: The dossier does not support eccentricity being the only such parameter — and the script itself contradicts this two paragraphs later. The Milankovitch reference hosted by Harvard (SOURCE 3) lists orbital inclination as one of Earth's movements, and the Muller & MacDonald PNAS paper (SOURCE 10) explicitly attributes the ~100-kyr cycle to orbital inclination rather than eccentricity. The same reference also notes eccentricity's variations are dominated by a 413,000-year term, with a number of other terms between 95,000 and 136,000 years that only loosely combine into a 100,000-year cycle — so eccentricity does not have a clean 100-kyr period either.
flags.suggested_fix: Of the three classic Milankovitch parameters, only eccentricity has variations anywhere near one hundred thousand years — and even there, the reference gives a set of terms between ninety-five thousand and one hundred thirty-six thousand years that only loosely combine into the beat.

flags.quote: And according to a 2008 study in Nature, that switch happened without any apparent change in the insolation forcing.
flags.detail: The substance is supported: the dossier's Nature paper 'North American ice-sheet dynamics and the onset of 100,000-year glacial cycles' says the transition from 41,000-year to 100,000-year cycles 'occurred without an apparent change in insolation forcing'. But the dossier never dates that paper. Its title and URL (nature07158) carry no year, unlike the other sources whose DOIs encode 2023/2025. The year 2008 is therefore an unsourced date in the script.
flags.suggested_fix: And according to a study in Nature, that switch happened without any apparent change in the insolation forcing. (Or add the full citation, with year, to the dossier so the date can be stated.)

flags.quote: This warm interval you are living in has run about ten thousand years.
flags.detail: No source is named in this sentence, and the dossier's two relevant sources give different figures. The USGS fact sheet says 'the current interglacial climate, which has lasted about 10,000 years'. The UC Santa Barbara report on the 2025 Science analysis says Earth emerged 'from the last glaciation around 11,700 years ago'. The script picks one figure without crediting it or acknowledging the disagreement.
flags.suggested_fix: According to the USGS, this warm interval has run about ten thousand years — though UC Santa Barbara dates the end of the last glaciation to around eleven thousand seven hundred years ago.
